[T]he argument is that while congress may create an office, it cannot 
appoint the officer; that the officer can only be appointed by the 
president, with the approval of the senate; and that the act itseK 
defines these park commissioners to be ‘pubhc officers,’ because it 
prescribes that three of them are to be civihans, to be nominated by 
the president and confirmed by the senate. This, it is said, is 
equivalent to a declaration by congress that the three so sent to the 
senate are ‘officers,’ because the constitution provides only for the 
nomination of officers to be sent to the senate for confirmation; and 
that it hence follows that the other two are likewise officers, whose 
appointment should have been made by the president and confirmed 
by the senate. As, however, the two persons whose efigibifity is 
questioned were at the time of the passage of the act and of their 
action under it officers of the United States who had been theretofore 
appointed by the president, and confiLrmed by the senate, we do not 
think that, because additional duties, germane to the offices already 
held by them, were devolved upon them by the act, it was necessary 
that they should be again appointed by the president and confirmed 
by the senate. It cannot be doubted, and it has frequently been the 
case, that congress may increase the power and duties of an existing 
office without thereby rendering it necessary that the incumbent 
should be again nominated and appointed.
It is true that it may be sometimes difficult to say whether a 
given duty, devolved by statute upon a named officer, has regard to 
the civil or military service of the United States. But, in the present 
case, the duty which the military officers in question were called upon 
to perform cannot fairly be said to have been dissimilar to, or outside 
of the sphere of, their official duties.
147 U.S. at 300-301.
The Court reached the same conclusion in Weiss v. United States, 510 U.S. 
163 (1994), which rejected a challenge to the method of appointing military 
trial and appellate judges. Mihtary judges are commissioned military officers 
who are selected and certified as qualified by the Judge Advocate General of 
their branch of the Armed Forces. The Coujrt determined that there was “no 
ground for suspicion here that Congress was trying to both create an office and 
also select a particular individual to fill the office.” Further, the assignment of 
new duties satisfied the requirement of “germaneness” the Court had 
identified in Shoemaker. The Court concluded that “all mihtary officers, 
consistent with a long tradition, play a role in the operation of the mihtary 
justice system,” and the duties of mihtary judges more closely resemble the 
sorts of special duties often assigned to commissioned officers than the duties 
normahy associated with judges in a civihan context. Hence, they could take 
on those duties without an additional appointment.
